reading.rtitle: The Median Tells You Less Than You Think
paras: Every executive program publishes a page of numbers about the people it admits, and the page always looks like a description. It is not. It is a recruiting document, written for the candidate who is trying to work out whether they belong, and every figure on it has been chosen with that reader in mind. That is not a criticism; it is what the page is for. It does mean, though, that reading it as a neutral report is the first mistake a candidate makes.

Start with the median, which these pages almost always use instead of the average, and for a good reason. Two or three participants with unusually long careers are enough to pull an average upwards, and once it moves everybody else looks junior by comparison. The median does not move. It is the middle case, and the outliers sit on either side of it without touching it. A page that gives you a median and a range is answering two different questions at once: where the middle of the room is, and how wide the room is.

The sector breakdown is the part candidates read backwards. Financial services accounts for around a quarter of a typical cohort and construction for something closer to four per cent, and the candidate from construction reads that four as a warning. Admissions offices say the opposite, and they say it in public: they are building a room, and a sector at four per cent is one they are short of. Being underrepresented is not evidence that you do not fit. It is the reason the conversation is worth having, provided you can say what you would bring that the other ninety-six per cent cannot.

listenings.text: People treat the class profile as if it were a report on us, and it is not. It is a recruiting document. It is written for the candidate who is sitting at a kitchen table trying to work out whether they belong here, and every number on it was chosen with that person in mind. Now, why the median and not the average. Because two or three people with very long careers pull the average up, and the moment it moves, everybody else on the page looks junior. The median does not move. It is the middle case, and the outliers sit on either side without touching it. And here is the thing I would most like candidates from smaller sectors to hear, because we say it publicly and almost nobody believes us. They look at four per cent and read it as a warning. It is the opposite. We are building a room, and a sector at four per cent is one we are short of.

I will tell you what I got wrong, because I spent about a month on it. I assumed everybody would be from finance or consulting, that their English would be better than mine, and that I would be the only person in the room who had never worked outside his own country. Three weeks in, none of that had survived contact with reality. Roughly a third of the room is not American. Several of them are considerably harder to understand than I am, and I say that with affection. And nobody cares. What I did not expect is what actually made me stand out. It was not the accent and it was certainly not my finance vocabulary. It was that I run a company I own, and that I have been in it for twenty-two years, which in that room is unusual. I spent the first month trying to sound like the people from finance, and it was a month I would like back.
